persons.note: A CONTEMPORARY CHICAGO PAPER OF 1833-1835 PRINTS THIS PERSON BY NAME IN THE TOWN. Read from newspaper_1833_1835. THE GRADE IS THE OWNER'S RATIFIED LADDER OF 2026-09-03 (G1b), applied to every identity at once by tools/consolidate_resident_evidence.py and spent onto this card by tools/mint_civic_residents.py; the evidence blocks below carry the reading AS READ, its locator and the record it came from, so the page can be gone back to. WHAT IS RECONSTRUCTED: everything except the person and the sources — no dwelling, no trade, no origin, no family, no party. A BOUND FROM THE RECORD, NOT AN ARRIVAL. newspaper_1833_1835 names this person at Chicago by 11 July 1835 and nothing says when they came. THE BOUND FALLS AFTER THE SCENE DATE and the record says so rather than narrowing it: the earliest source that names this person is later than 1 July 1835, so they may have arrived after the day this scene models. present_on_scene_date is `uncertain` for that reason. No figure is drawn (L1). THE FEDERAL LAND TRACT SALES — A PURCHASE, AND NEVER A RESIDENCE. The Illinois State Archives' Public Domain Land Tract Sales register enters this person 3 times, as “CLARK JOHN K”, 1834-11-04: 2 federal land entries — E2SE sec 06 T39N R14E; SW sec 11 T40N R13E, 240.00 acres stated in all, for $300.00 (ls0026, ls0027, ls0897). THE REGISTER'S OWN RESIDENCE COLUMN READS COOK, UNKNOWN on these rows: a county, a state or nothing, and never a town, which is why a purchase here places nobody. The register states this purchaser's residence as COOK, so the sale is contemporary evidence that a man of this name lived in Cook County on the date of sale. It is not evidence that he lived in the town. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: CLARK JOHN K matches John K Clark: the forename names John K Clark of the 4 people of this surname, and the forename agrees in full. (data/research/land_sales/resident_crosswalk.json). This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) a second independent source is what lifts a projected resident, and a land entry is a second source about a TRANSACTION rather than about who was living at Chicago on 1 July 1835 — a man may buy a quarter-section he never sees. T-0515 applies the ladder against every source at once; this pass hands it the evidence and not the verdict.

merge_ruling.for_merge: 'Chark' is one letter from Clark, h for l, and the forename 'John A.' agrees letter for letter with John K. Clark, in the American of 11 July 1835 (#c007). The stem 'Chark' is set nowhere in the deposited corpus and the town holds no other bearer of it: on the face of it a card minted off a garble.
merge_ruling.against_merge: A GARBLED READING CANNOT BE TESTED, AND THERE ARE TWO CLARKS IT COULD BE. R5 is the standing refusal and T-0695 is the ticket that reads these cards at the image; T-1027 files `chark_john_a` under the garbles in its own words — 'a fold here would repair a wreck by guessing at it'. The guess is not even single-valued: the town holds clark_john_a and clark_john_k, and the `clark-john` cluster has already ruled those two DISTINCT under D1 on their contradicting middle initials, so a fold of 'John A. Chark' would have to choose which of two ruled-apart men to join. Clark is set 2,655 times in the corpus and the reading index holds 37 Clark identities. R5, and the reading belongs to T-0695.

Both cards print an explicit middle initial and the two disagree — A against K — with no anchor on either side to say one of them is mis-set. Two men until something says otherwise, and the ruling is written onto both cards so the next pass does not re-ask.

directories.note: LATER EVIDENCE, BESIDE THE 1835 CLAIMS AND NOT INSIDE THEM. A Chicago directory of 1839, 1843 or 1844 meets somebody of this name and this pass records what it prints.
